title: The Concession That Invented Modern Oil
event_summary: William Knox D'Arcy, a wealthy British speculator who had never visited Persia, signed a sixty-year concession with Shah Mozaffar ad-Din that granted him exclusive rights to prospect for and exploit petroleum across nearly 500,000 square miles — three-quarters of Persia's territory — in exchange for £20,000 in cash, £20,000 in shares, and a 16% royalty. The deal was brokered by Antoine Kitabgi, a Georgian-born Persian customs official who had been quietly lobbying European investors. This single document became the template for every oil concession in the Middle East for the next half-century, eventually giving birth to the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later known as BP.
why_forgotten: The concession is overshadowed by the dramatic 1953 CIA-backed coup against Mossadegh, which most people learn as the origin of oil conflict in Iran. D'Arcy himself died in relative obscurity in 1917, and Kitabgi's pivotal intermediary role was deliberately minimized by British interests who preferred a narrative of Western technological initiative rather than local collaboration. The lopsided terms were also an embarrassment that neither side wished to highlight.
why_it_matters: The D'Arcy Concession established the legal and financial architecture — fixed royalties, vast territorial grants, decades-long exclusivity — that would define oil extraction across Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and the Gulf states, shaping the entire geopolitics of energy. Its eventual nationalization by Mossadegh in 1951 triggered the first great confrontation between resource sovereignty and Western corporate power, a template still replayed today in disputes from Venezuela to Libya. The modern petrostate, OPEC, and the West's entanglement with Middle Eastern politics all trace back to this single contract signed in a Tehran palace.
